title: Thermal stress reduces dung burial, brood production, and the development of dung beetles: a challenge for climate resilience
content:
Abstract
Increasing temperatures can impair ecosystem services and the reproduction of dung beetles. We investigated the effects of increased nest temperatures on reproduction, dung burial, and the development of 2 dung beetle species (Onthophagus binodis and Digitonthophagus gazella). Three pairs of sexually mature F1-beetles at 15 days of age were housed in temperature-controlled chambers for 2 weeks. Temperature treatments of +3 °C and +5 °C above baseline (control: a diurnal temperature cycle modelled from 2019 to 2023 summer data at the beetles origin location) were applied. Fresh cattle dung was provided to feed the beetles, and the dung burial was recorded weekly. The number of broods produced, brood success, developmental days, pronotum width, and body weight of F2 progeny were recorded. Relative to the baseline treatment, brood production was reduced by 43.1% at +3 °C and 39.3% at +5 °C, with no significant difference between the 2 elevated-temperature treatments. Dung burial was 96 g/kg dry matter lower when beetles were reared at +3 °C compared to the control. Increased temperature did not affect brood success; however, the highest nest temperature reduced the development time of D. gazella by 2.45 days compared to the control or the +3 °C treatment. In addition, a mixed effect of the highest temperature was observed in the pronotum width, which was 0.49 mm smaller and 0.32 mm greater in the F2 beetles of O. binodis and D. gazella, respectively, compared to those that were reared with +3 °C. In conclusion, heat stress negatively affected brood construction, reduced dung burial and development of F2 progeny, and altered pronotum width, suggesting that climate warming may compromise dung beetle-mediated ecosystem services such as dung removal and associated nutrient cycling.
